headline: High: Kestra can write and exfiltrate while Caveman can ingest shared files/MCP, creating dangerous default-path interaction risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Caveman uses MCP and reads/writes project files, while Kestra can read/write filesystem and pass data through workflows. A shared file or MCP bridge could let attacker-controlled content from Kestra influence Caveman prompts. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so the interaction is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF Caveman ingests Kestra-produced files or MCP messages as instructions
IF Kestra writes attacker-controlled content into a shared workspace
mitigations: Restrict Caveman to a read-only prompt directory
Separate Kestra and Caveman workspaces
Add provenance tags to all shared files
Disable MCP bridges for untrusted content
requires-engineering: enforce content sanitization before prompt ingestion

B_data_leakage.rationale: Caveman touches session logs, memory files, project notes, and CLAUDE.md, while Kestra has broad network egress and can move data to email, Slack, cloud, and databases. If they share a workspace, sensitive local artifacts from Caveman can be picked up and transmitted by Kestra by default. The blast radius includes exfiltration of logs and notes.
conditions: IF Caveman stores secrets or notes in shared files
IF Kestra workflows read those files and send them to external APIs
mitigations: Move Caveman artifacts to a private directory
Block Kestra access to Caveman memory/log files
Disable outbound connectors for sensitive workflows
Review workflow inputs for secrets before execution
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction on workflow inputs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Caveman supports multiple instances and writes project files, while Kestra also writes filesystem state and can spawn subprocesses with elevated privileges. On a shared directory, concurrent writes can corrupt files or overwrite workflow artifacts. Because no locking or coordination is documented, uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory
IF Kestra tasks modify files that Caveman also edits
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Use file locks around shared artifacts
Run one agent at a time for shared paths
Make shared files append-only
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Caveman is a content-writing agent and Kestra is an automation/orchestration system with email, Slack, and cloud actions. If Kestra treats Caveman output as authoritative, a mistaken draft can become an automated downstream action. That creates a direct path from generated text to irreversible operational effects.
conditions: IF Kestra uses Caveman output as workflow input without verification
IF a workflow task sends emails, notifications, or cloud actions based on that output
mitigations: Insert a human approval step before actions
Require schema validation on Caveman outputs
Limit automation to dry-run mode
Log and diff generated instructions before execution
requires-engineering: add policy gates for high-impact tasks

E_compliance.rationale: Caveman stores session logs, memory files, and project notes, while Kestra handles logs, inputs, variables, artifacts, and database/cloud data. If the same regulated data class flows through both, differing retention or residency policies can create a compliance mismatch. No specific certification gap is documented, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in Caveman artifacts and then processed by Kestra
IF retention or residency rules differ between the two systems
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent
Keep regulated data out of shared artifacts
Set matching retention windows
Document residency for each workflow
requires-engineering: align compliance controls across both systems
